python-for-ops-fundamentals.core: Python is the glue language of the cloud. It handles structured data, talks to APIs reliably, isolates its dependencies and turns logs into answers, all with readable, testable code.

first_principles.problem: Ops automation outgrows Bash once it involves JSON, many APIs, retries and data analysis.
truths: Automation must be reproducible and robust.

analogy.title: A universal adapter
analogy.story: Python plugs into every system (AWS, HTTP APIs, log files) through a library made for each.
analogy.breaks: For tiny shell tasks Python is overkill, and Bash is still fine there.

example.title: Nightly cost-report script
example.scenario: Combines every lesson in this topic.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: A reproducible, robust report with no fragile parsing.

example.outcome: Python is the dependable layer of ops automation.

check.q: Name two practices that make a Python ops script robust.
check.a: Timeouts with retries and backoff on HTTP calls, and pinned dependencies in a venv.

bash-mastery-advanced-scripting.core: Advanced Bash is about composing Unix tools safely: streams and pipes move the data, exit codes drive the logic, strict mode and traps add safety, expansions and arrays handle data in-process, and tracing makes bugs visible.

first_principles.problem: Naive scripts fail silently, leave messes, break on spaces and are painful to debug.
truths: Every command reports success or failure.
Spaces and empty variables are the classic bugs.

analogy.title: Building a reliable production line
analogy.story: Conveyors (pipes), quality gates (exit codes), circuit breakers (strict mode), cleanup crews (traps) and inspection cameras (set -x).
analogy.breaks: Bash is still the wrong tool for complex logic. Switch languages once a script outgrows it.

example.title: A production-grade backup script

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: It fails fast, cleans up, handles spaces and requires its inputs.

code.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT
paths=(/etc "/srv/my data")
tar czf "$TMP/b.tgz" "${paths[@]}" 2>>"$LOG"
aws s3 cp "$TMP/b.tgz" "s3://${BUCKET:?}/$(date +%F).tgz"

example.outcome: Bash scripts you can run unattended with confidence.

check.q: Which three settings form Bash strict mode?
check.a: set -e, set -u and set -o pipefail.

git-internals-under-the-hood.core: Git is a content-addressed store of snapshot objects (blobs, trees, commits) plus movable refs. Merging, rebasing, bisecting and the reflog are all operations on that graph and its pointers.

first_principles.problem: Treating Git as magic leads to fear, lost work and messy history.
truths: Content is addressed by its hash.
Branches and HEAD are just pointers.

analogy.title: A city map with movable pins
analogy.story: The streets (commits) never change once built. You move pins (branches) around, and a logbook (reflog) remembers where every pin used to be.
analogy.breaks: Rebase builds new streets rather than moving old ones, which is why rewritten history gets new hashes.

example.title: A bad week, recovered

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Each problem is solved by reasoning about objects and pointers.

example.outcome: Git becomes predictable and recoverable.

check.q: Why is it hard to lose committed work in Git?
check.a: Objects persist and the reflog remembers old pointer positions until garbage collection.

branching-strategies-gitflow-trunk-based.core: A branching strategy is the team's agreement on balancing isolation against integration. GitFlow suits scheduled releases, GitHub Flow suits continuous deployment, and trunk-based development with feature flags integrates continuously.

first_principles.problem: Without an agreed model, branches drift, conflicts explode and the state of production is unclear.
truths: Merge pain grows with how long branches live.
Release cadence decides how much structure you need.
Deploying and releasing can be separated.
derivation: Choose a **repo layout** that fits your coupling.

analogy.title: Traffic systems
analogy.story: GitFlow is scheduled rail timetables, GitHub Flow is a single-lane road with checkpoints, and TBD is a continuously flowing roundabout.
analogy.breaks: Real teams mix them, for example TBD with short-lived release branches.

example.title: Choosing for three teams
example.scenario: Mobile app, SaaS web app, platform monorepo.

steps.label: Principle
steps.detail: Strategy follows release cadence.

example.outcome: each team integrates at the right speed.

check.q: Which strategy best fits deploying many times per day?
check.a: GitHub Flow or trunk-based development with feature flags.

cli-engineering-best-practices.core: CLI engineering turns personal scripts into dependable tools: conventional interfaces, layered configuration, output that serves both humans and machines, guarded destructive actions, honest exit codes and graceful shutdown.

first_principles.problem: Shared scripts with quirky interfaces and silent failures break pipelines and endanger production.
truths: Tools serve both humans and programs.
Automation depends on exit codes and stable output.
derivation: Signal **status** with exit codes and signal handling.

analogy.title: A well-designed appliance
analogy.story: Standard plugs (conventions), a clear display (output), a child lock (confirmations) and a safe power-off (signals).
analogy.breaks: Over-engineering a throwaway script wastes time. Apply this to shared tools.

example.title: Building 'svcctl'

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: It's safe for humans, scriptable and honest about results.

code.text:
svcctl restart api --env prod          # prompts
svcctl restart api --env prod --yes -o json | jq .status
echo $?   # 0 ok, 3 unhealthy

example.outcome: tools that teams and pipelines can trust.

check.q: Why separate stdout and stderr in a CLI?
check.a: So machine-readable data can be piped cleanly while messages still reach the human.

go-golang-for-ops.core: Go fits ops because it pairs simple syntax with cheap concurrency (goroutines, channels, context), explicit errors, typed JSON, implicit interfaces and single static binaries that cross-compile anywhere.

first_principles.problem: Ops tools must run on many machines, make many concurrent network calls and fail clearly, which strains scripting languages.
truths: Distribution and concurrency are central ops needs.
Cloud-native tooling is written in Go.
derivation: Fan out with **goroutines**, collect with **channels**, bound with **context**.

analogy.title: A Swiss army knife made for networks
analogy.story: Compact, self-contained and built to do many things at once.
analogy.breaks: For quick one-off data munging, Python is often faster to write.

example.title: A fleet health checker

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: 500 hosts in about 5 seconds from one copied file.

example.outcome: fast, safe, easily distributed ops tooling.

check.q: Which Go features prevent a tool from hanging on a dead host?
check.a: context.WithTimeout passed to calls, combined with select on ctx.Done().

rust-for-infrastructure-basics.core: Rust offers memory safety without a garbage collector through compile-time ownership and borrowing, async concurrency through Tokio, and fully static binaries. It fits infrastructure components where performance and correctness are critical.

first_principles.problem: Some infrastructure (proxies, agents, runtimes) needs C-like speed without C's memory bugs.
truths: Memory bugs are the top source of security vulnerabilities.

analogy.title: A precision tool with built-in guards
analogy.story: It cuts as fast as the most dangerous saw, but the guard physically stops you misusing it.
analogy.breaks: The guards slow beginners down. Rust is overkill for simple scripts.

example.title: A log-shipping agent

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Low CPU and memory on thousands of nodes.

example.outcome: Rust handles performance-critical infrastructure safely.

check.q: What enforces Rust's memory safety?
check.a: The compiler's ownership and borrow-checking rules.

advanced-testing-pbt-fuzzing-mocks-docke.core: Advanced testing goes beyond hand-picked examples: property-based tests check invariants over generated inputs and shrink failures, fuzzers attack parsers with chaos, test doubles isolate logic (used sparingly), and containerised integration tests check reality.

first_principles.problem: Example tests miss edge cases, over-mocked tests break on refactors, and fakes hide integration bugs.
truths: Tests should check behaviour, not structure.
derivation: Use **PBT** for invariants, and let **shrinking** minimise failures.

analogy.title: Testing a car
analogy.story: Track tests (examples), random terrain (PBT), crash tests (fuzzing), a simulator (mocks) and a real road (Docker integration).
analogy.breaks: Each technique costs time, so use a pyramid: many fast tests and a few realistic ones.

example.title: Testing a URL-shortener service

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Each layer catches a different class of bug.

example.outcome: tests find bugs that humans wouldn't think to write.

check.q: Which technique best finds crashes in a binary protocol parser?
check.a: Coverage-guided fuzzing.

innersource-principles-and-practice.core: InnerSource brings open-source collaboration inside the company: visible code, contributions over tickets, clear governance, real incentives, discoverable components, budgeted maintenance and trusted committers who scale review.

first_principles.problem: Silos cause duplicated work and bottlenecks, while naive openness causes chaos and burnout.

analogy.title: A city's public library system
analogy.story: Open shelves (code), rules (governance), library cards and rewards (incentives), a catalogue (discoverability), staff budgets (maintenance) and volunteer librarians (trusted committers).
analogy.breaks: Culture change is slow, and tools alone don't create collaboration.

example.title: Launching an InnerSource programme

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Less duplication and faster unblocking.

example.outcome: teams collaborate like an open-source community.

check.q: Name two prerequisites for InnerSource beyond opening repositories.
check.a: For example, governance (contribution rules and owners) and incentives that reward contributing.

advanced-git-workflows.core: Advanced Git workflows handle the hard cases: worktrees for parallel checkouts (managed properly), bisect run for automated regression hunting, rerere for recurring conflicts, and submodules vs subtrees for embedding shared code.

first_principles.problem: Hotfixes mid-feature, mystery regressions, repeated conflicts and shared code cost the most time with basic Git.
truths: Git has purpose-built tools for each case.
Embedding code is a trade-off between pinning and convenience.
derivation: Work in parallel with **worktree** and clean up with **remove/prune**.

analogy.title: A craftsperson's specialised tools
analogy.story: A second bench (worktree), a metal detector (bisect run), a jig (rerere) and a choice between borrowing or copying a blueprint (submodule vs subtree).
analogy.breaks: These tools are power features. Most days, basic Git is enough.

example.title: A platform team's toolkit

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Hours saved weekly.

example.outcome: Git handles complex workflows smoothly.

check.q: Submodule or subtree for exact version pinning with separate history?
check.a: Submodule.

python-internals-ops.core: Python internals matter once code becomes a long-running system. The GIL determines which concurrency model works, context managers guarantee cleanup, decorators and metaclasses add behaviour and structure, and type hints with mypy catch bugs statically.

first_principles.problem: Production Python fails in ways scripts never do: no speed-up from threads, leaked resources, duplicated cross-cutting code and type bugs.
truths: The runtime has specific concurrency rules.
derivation: **GIL**: threads for I/O, processes for CPU.

analogy.title: Understanding a building's systems
analogy.story: Electrical limits (GIL), automatic doors (context managers), add-on fixtures (decorators), architectural codes (metaclasses) and inspections (mypy).
analogy.breaks: Over-engineering with metaclasses and deep decorator stacks hurts readability.

example.title: Hardening a deploy daemon

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: It's faster, leak-free, consistent and safely refactorable.

example.outcome: Python systems that stay healthy for months.

check.q: For a CPU-bound task, threads or processes?
check.a: Processes, because the GIL stops threads running Python bytecode in parallel.

go-advanced-patterns-reflection-unsafe-c.core: Go's advanced patterns are escape hatches: reflection for runtime type work (slow, risky), unsafe for raw memory (dangerous), cgo for C libraries (it costs portability), plus workspaces for multi-module development. Use each deliberately and keep it isolated.

first_principles.problem: Overusing escape hatches erodes Go's safety, speed and simple deployment.
truths: Each hatch trades away a guarantee.
derivation: Prefer **generics, interfaces or codegen** over reflection.
Use **unsafe** only with benchmarks proving the need.

analogy.title: A toolkit with locked drawers
analogy.story: The everyday tools are out on the bench; the dangerous ones are locked away, labelled and used rarely.
analogy.breaks: Libraries you use often contain these hatches already, well tested by their authors.

example.title: Reviewing a PR that adds cgo
flow: Is it isolated in one package?

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: The hatch is used only if it's justified.

example.outcome: Go stays safe and simple except where it truly can't.

check.q: What's the biggest deployment cost of cgo?
check.a: Losing easy cross-compilation and fully static binaries.

resiliency-patterns-from-scratch.core: Resilient code assumes failure: exponential backoff with jitter absorbs transient errors without a stampede, circuit breakers fail fast during sustained outages, and bulkheads stop one dependency from exhausting shared resources. Timeouts underpin all three.

first_principles.problem: Without containment, any one dependency failure cascades into a full outage.

analogy.title: A ship's safety systems
analogy.story: Wave timing (backoff), engine cut-offs (circuit breakers) and watertight compartments (bulkheads) keep the ship afloat in a storm.
analogy.breaks: Patterns interact. For example, retries inside an open circuit are wasted, so design them together.

example.title: A checkout service under stress

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: A degraded experience instead of an outage.

example.outcome: failures stay contained.

check.q: Which pattern handles a dependency down for 10 minutes?
check.a: The circuit breaker: fail fast and probe periodically for recovery.

supply-chain-security-code-level.core: Supply-chain security means distrusting your inputs by default: pin with lockfiles and hashes, scan continuously (SCA), block dependency confusion, route through a private registry, inventory with SBOMs and verify build provenance with SLSA.

first_principles.problem: Attackers poison dependencies and build systems because a single compromise reaches every downstream user.

analogy.title: Food safety from farm to table
analogy.story: Sealed batches, recall alerts, approved suppliers, a central warehouse, ingredient labels and chain-of-custody records.
analogy.breaks: No layer is complete on its own, so defence in depth is the point.

example.title: Hardening a CI pipeline

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Tampering is detected at several points.

example.outcome: dependencies and builds are verifiable.

check.q: Which control specifically defends against a compromised build server?
check.a: SLSA provenance from an isolated builder, with signature verification before deploy.

dev-environments-containers-nix.core: Reproducible development environments end 'it works on my machine'. Dev Containers package the toolchain in a container behind your IDE, and Nix builds exact, hash-pinned toolchains natively. Choose by team skill and how much reproducibility you need, and reuse the definition in CI.

first_principles.problem: Manual setup drifts, so onboarding is slow and bugs are environment-specific.

analogy.title: Standardised workshops
analogy.story: Every engineer walks into an identical workshop, either rented and furnished (container) or built from exact blueprints (Nix).
analogy.breaks: Environments still need updates. Pinning freezes bugs as well as versions.

example.title: A platform repo setup
flow: CI runs nix develop -c make test

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: One definition serves laptops, Codespaces and CI.

example.outcome: environment bugs disappear.

check.q: What's the core idea shared by Dev Containers and Nix?
check.a: Defining the development environment declaratively as code in the repository.

polyglot-interoperability-protobuf-ffi.core: Polyglot systems need a common contract: Protobuf schemas for compact, typed, evolvable messages between services, or FFI over the C ABI for fast calls within one process, with explicit care for memory and crash safety.

first_principles.problem: Mixed-language stacks suffer from drifting contracts, slow serialisation and unsafe native calls.
truths: Each language has its own types.
Network calls cost far more than in-process calls.
derivation: Define **ownership** at boundaries and isolate risk.

analogy.title: International trade
analogy.story: Standard shipping containers (Protobuf) move goods between countries, and a direct pipeline (FFI) is faster but needs strict safety rules.
analogy.breaks: Too much FFI couples languages tightly, while too many RPCs add latency.

example.title: An ML feature pipeline
flow: Go API ⇄ Python service via gRPC

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Typed contracts and native speed where it matters.

example.outcome: languages cooperate safely and efficiently.

check.q: What makes Protobuf schemas safely evolvable?
check.a: Numbered fields: new fields can be added and unknown ones ignored, as long as numbers are never reused.

semver-conventional-commits.core: Release communication is a pipeline: SemVer gives version numbers meaning, Conventional Commits make history machine-readable, automation turns history into versions and changelogs, and commitlint keeps the input clean.

first_principles.problem: Ad-hoc versions and messy commits make upgrades scary and release notes unreliable.

analogy.title: A postal system
analogy.story: Standard addresses (commits) let sorting machines (automation) route mail (versions), and the counter rejects badly addressed letters (commitlint).
analogy.breaks: Automation can't judge whether something is really breaking. Humans must label it honestly.

example.title: A library's release flow

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Zero manual versioning, and trustworthy upgrades.

example.outcome: releases speak a clear, automated language.

check.q: How does `feat!:` affect the next version?
check.a: It marks a breaking change, so the MAJOR version is bumped.

ai-assisted-engineering-copilot-cursor.core: AI-assisted engineering turns the engineer into a director: choose the right tool (autocomplete vs agent), write context-rich prompts, review output as a first draft, manage legal and data risks, and apply AI where it's strong.

first_principles.problem: AI can speed delivery or quietly inject bugs, security holes and licence risk, depending on how it's used.
truths: AI output is plausible, not guaranteed correct.

analogy.title: Flying with autopilot
analogy.story: Autopilot handles routine flight, but the pilot plans the route, monitors constantly and takes over in turbulence.
analogy.breaks: Over-reliance can erode skills, so keep practising the fundamentals.

example.title: Building a CLI with AI help

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Faster delivery with quality intact.

example.outcome: AI amplifies engineers instead of replacing their judgement.

check.q: Why treat AI output as a first draft?
check.a: It can be confidently wrong (hallucinated APIs, insecure patterns), and the engineer is accountable for merged code.

vscode-ide-mastery.core: Mastering VS Code means using it as a platform. Its client/server architecture (LSP, DAP) enables real debugging with launch.json and remote development over SSH or in containers, while curated extensions and snippets keep it fast and productive.

first_principles.problem: Using VS Code as a plain editor wastes debugging, remote and automation features that ops work needs.

analogy.title: A pilot's cockpit
analogy.story: Instruments (LSP), black-box recorder (debugger), remote control of drones (remote dev), only the necessary gauges (curated extensions) and autopilot presets (snippets).
analogy.breaks: Setup takes time, so invest in the features you'll use repeatedly.

example.title: A tuned ops workspace

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: New teammates get the full setup on clone.

example.outcome: an IDE configured as shared, versioned infrastructure.

check.q: Which protocol lets VS Code debug many languages with one UI?
check.a: The Debug Adapter Protocol (DAP).

code-review-etiquette.core: Effective code review is technical and social: kind, specific feedback about the code; labelled severity; authors who send small, well-described PRs; fast responses; and automation that handles style so humans focus on logic.

first_principles.problem: Harsh, slow or nitpicky reviews damage morale and slow delivery without improving quality.

analogy.title: A healthy sports team's film review
analogy.story: Specific, kind and prompt feedback on plays (not players), with stats tracked automatically.
analogy.breaks: Culture comes from behaviour. Leaders must model it.

example.title: A model review

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: High quality, low friction.

example.outcome: reviews build both code quality and team trust.

check.q: What should human reviewers focus on when style is automated?
check.a: Logic, design, security, edge cases and clarity of intent.

ast-parsing-custom-linters.core: Custom linters parse code into an AST instead of regex-matching text, walk typed nodes to find patterns (resolving imports and attributes), plug into tools like Pylint, and enforce rules in pre-commit and CI with baselines for legacy code.

first_principles.problem: Team-specific rules (no requests without a timeout, no shell=True) can't be enforced reliably with grep.
truths: Precision requires context such as imports.

analogy.title: A building inspector with blueprints
analogy.story: Rather than scanning photos for shapes, they read the blueprint structure and check each component against code.
analogy.breaks: Static analysis can't see runtime-dynamic behaviour.

example.title: A security rule rollout

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: A risky pattern is eliminated permanently.

example.outcome: team knowledge becomes enforceable code.

check.q: What's the first step in writing an AST-based linter in Python?
check.a: Parsing the source into a tree with ast.parse.

semantic-code-search-zoekt-sourcegraph.core: Code search at scale replaces scanning with indexing: trigram indexes find candidates for any substring, literal extraction speeds up regex, structural search matches code shapes, and a sharded fan-out system with code intelligence serves the whole organisation.

first_principles.problem: grep can't answer questions across thousands of repositories fast enough to be useful.
truths: Scanning is linear in data size.
Code needs substring rather than word indexing.
Freshness and scale require a system design.

analogy.title: A search engine for a city's archives
analogy.story: Index cards for every letter-triplet, sieves before microscopes, many archive buildings searched in parallel.
analogy.breaks: Even indexed search can't answer runtime questions like 'what actually calls this in production'.

example.title: A large-scale API migration
flow: Search all callers of v1 client

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: The migration finishes in weeks instead of quarters.

example.outcome: code becomes navigable at organisation scale.

check.q: What data structure underpins Zoekt's fast substring search?
check.a: A trigram index (posting lists of 3-character substrings).

makefile-for-devops.core: A Makefile is the project's universal run button: rules with TAB recipes, .PHONY for action targets, layered variables for environment and CI injection, and patterns like a self-documenting help so every repo exposes the same simple commands.

first_principles.problem: Long, fragile, tribal-knowledge commands make projects hard to operate and CI hard to keep in sync.
truths: The same entry point for humans and CI prevents drift.
derivation: Write **rules** correctly (tabs, one shell per line).

analogy.title: A cockpit's labelled switch panel
analogy.story: Every procedure is one clearly labelled switch, the same for every pilot and the autopilot.
analogy.breaks: Make isn't a general-purpose language, so put complex logic in scripts.

example.title: A platform repo Makefile

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: One interface for every environment and person.

example.outcome: projects are operable by anyone.

check.q: What does a .PHONY declaration prevent?
check.a: Make skipping an action target because a file with the same name exists.

regex-deep-dive-lookarounds-atomic.core: Advanced regex makes patterns correct, safe and maintainable: lookaheads and lookbehinds match on context without consuming it, atomic groups and linear engines prevent catastrophic backtracking, and named and non-capturing groups keep patterns readable.

first_principles.problem: Basic regexes over-match on messy data, can be weaponised for ReDoS, and turn into unreadable line noise.

analogy.title: A professional's search toolkit
analogy.story: Context lenses (lookarounds), a circuit breaker (atomic) and labelled specimen jars (named groups).
analogy.breaks: For nested languages (HTML, JSON), use a parser instead.

example.title: A log-parsing rule for a SIEM

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: It extracts non-OK login and logout actions per user, safely and readably.

example.outcome: production-grade patterns.

check.q: Which construct prevents the engine backtracking into a group?
check.a: An atomic group (?>...) or a possessive quantifier.

git-hooks-server-side-policy.core: Server-side enforcement is the only reliable policy layer. pre-receive gates whole pushes, update applies per-branch rules and post-receive triggers automation, while hosted platforms provide the same through rulesets, required checks, push protection and webhooks.

first_principles.problem: Client hooks are optional and bypassable, so secrets, force-pushes and bad commits slip through.
truths: Every push passes through the server.
Hosted platforms expose policy as configuration.
derivation: On the cloud: **rulesets, required checks, push protection**.

analogy.title: A country's border system
analogy.story: Passport control (pre-receive), visa rules per destination (update) and welcome notifications after entry (post-receive).
analogy.breaks: Slow server checks hurt every developer, so keep them fast and give clear messages.

example.title: A complete policy setup
flow: Self-hosted: pre-receive secret scan + update no-force main + post-receive CI
GitHub: rulesets + push protection + required checks + Actions

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Policy that can't be skipped.

example.outcome: repositories enforce their own rules.

check.q: Which hook would you use to block secrets across all refs in a push?
check.a: pre-receive.

open-source-licensing-risk.core: Public code isn't free to use: licences grant rights with conditions. Permissive licences need attribution; copyleft (GPL, AGPL) requires sharing derivatives; combinations must be compatible; and enterprises manage all this with tiered policies and automated scanning.

first_principles.problem: Unchecked dependencies can force source disclosure or create legal liability.
truths: Compliance must be automated to scale.

analogy.title: Food sourcing for a restaurant chain
analogy.story: Know each supplier's terms, avoid ingredients with onerous conditions, check allergen combinations and use an approved-supplier system.
analogy.breaks: Not legal advice. Policies must be set with counsel.

example.title: A new product's licence compliance

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Clean releases with minimal friction.

example.outcome: open source is used confidently and legally.

check.q: Which licence family requires derivatives to use the same licence?
check.a: Copyleft (e.g. GPL).
